cells.tense: The care and the direction are moving together right now
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're keeping alive and tell one person today what you did this week to keep it that way — small is fine, they don't have to ask.
cells.core:
There are things in front of you that you're keeping alive on purpose — the habit, the relationship, the work, the daily effort nobody sees. You know which demand is loudest and which one actually needs you, and you've stopped letting the loud one win by default. What you feed grows, and you're feeding the right things.

The part that's easy to miss is that you're doing this well and getting no acknowledgment for it, from anyone including yourself. What comes back when you say out loud what you've been carrying — the specific thing, the specific week — is a kind of release that finishing something alone doesn't give you. Say it once to someone who'll hear it.

cells.tense: You're watering ground that hasn't been planted yet
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and close the loop on it today — send the email, make the call, file the thing — then leave it alone for the rest of the day.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day, you know what's alive and what needs water, and you do the next right thing without checking the whole plot. You make your choices and you sleep.

Right now you're pouring into things that haven't arrived — the future version of the relationship, the version of the work where it finally lands, the crisis that might happen. The effort is real, but the thing hasn't asked for it yet, and you're spending today's water on next season. This has stopped answering to what's actually in front of it. Finishing one actual thing, today, in the world, gives the pull something solid to land on.

cells.tense: You walked past a thing you were keeping alive and kept walking
cells.ask: Go back to one thing you set down and do one small act of care on it in the next hour — water it, email it, put it back where you can see it.
cells.core:
In ordinary weeks, you return to what pulls you — the idea you keep coming back to, the person you check on, the practice that holds you up — and the returning is what keeps the pull alive. Not forcing it, just showing up.

What's happening now is that the pull is still there, but your hands have gone quiet on it. Something that used to be in front of you got set down, and picking it back up feels like it costs more than it should. What you wanted hasn't left; the showing up stopped. Pushing harder at the starved thing won't bring it back. Picking up one small habit that used to keep you close to it will.

cells.tense: You're already keeping it alive and calling it something else
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been keeping alive lately — the actual time, the actual effort — and say out loud to someone that you did it on purpose.
cells.core:
On a good week, you keep what matters alive without making a speech about it — the friendship you check on, the work nobody assigned, the small habit that holds the week together — and you know quietly that your hand is in it.

The same is happening now, except that quiet certainty has gone missing. These things keep going because you keep going back to them, and you describe it like it happens on its own, or like it's just what's required. The effort goes unrecognized by the one person who'd most benefit from seeing it. Saying it plain, to someone, puts the work back where it belongs — in your hands.
